segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After the uproar had died down, Paul sent for the disciples and encouraged them; then he said farewell and set out to go to Macedonia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After travelling through those parts and encouraging the people there with many words, he came to Greece

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and spent three months there. When a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus, from Beroea; by Aristarchus and Secundus, from Thessalonica; by Gaius from Derbe, and Timothy; and by Tychicus and Trophimus, from Asia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These men came and were waiting for us at Troas;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but we sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and within five days came to them at Troas, where we stayed seven days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul was addressing them. Since he was going to leave the next day, he kept on speaking until midnight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were gathered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A young man named Eutychus was sitting on the windowsill, sinking into a deep sleep as Paul went on speaking at length. Overcome by sleep, he fell from the third story to the ground below and was picked up dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Paul went down, threw himself on him, and putting his arms around him said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went back up, broke the bread and ate, and after talking with them a long while, until dawn, he left.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They took the boy away alive, and were comforted more than a little.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As for us, we went ahead to the ship and set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul on board there; for that is what he had arranged, since he himself intended to travel by land.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he met us at Assos, we took him on board and came to Mitylene.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Sailing from there, we arrived the next day off Chios; the day after, we crossed over to Samos; and the day after that, we came to Miletus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he would not have to spend time in Asia; he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem, if it were possible for him, on the day of Pentecost.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came to him, he said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You yourselves know how, from the first day I set foot in Asia, I was with you the whole time,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: serving the Lord as a slave with all humility, with tears, and with the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: how I did not hold back from declaring to you anything that would benefit you, and from teaching you in public and from house to house,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: testifying solemnly to both Jews and Greeks about turning back to God and faith in our Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now, look, bound by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: except that the Holy Spirit testifies solemnly to me in city after city, saying that chains and afflictions await me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But I do not count my life worth anything or precious to myself, so long as I complete my course and the service I received from the Lord Jesus: to testify solemnly to the good news of God’s grace.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now, look, I know that all of you, among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom, will not see my face again.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Therefore I testify to you this very day that I am clean of the blood of all,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for I did not hold back from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Keep watch over yourselves and over the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as overseers, to shepherd the assembly of God, which he acquired through the blood of his Own.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I know that after my departure savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and from among your own selves men will arise speaking twisted things, to draw the disciples away after them.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Therefore stay awake, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not stop warning each one of you with tears.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who have been made holy.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You yourselves know that these hands served my own needs and those of the people with me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In everything I showed you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak, and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had said these things, he knelt down with them all and prayed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was much weeping from them all; they threw their arms around Paul’s neck and kissed him again and again,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: grieving most of all over the word he had spoken, that they were not going to see his face again. Then they escorted him to the ship.

notes.note: Asia here and throughout the chapter is the Roman province of that name, the western part of modern Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city. It is not the continent.

The manuscripts are divided between two verbs that differ by a single letter: 'having come' and 'having gone ahead'. The Greek text translated here prints the first; many editions and most English versions follow the second. The sense of the passage is little affected.

The narrative switches here to the first person plural, which it last used at Philippi in chapter 16. The usual explanation is that the author, or a source he draws on, rejoined Paul's party at Philippi. The nature of these 'we' passages remains debated.

notes.phrase: On the first day of the week
notes.note: The Greek idiom is literally 'the first of the sabbaths', the day after the Sabbath. It is disputed whether Luke counts days from sunset, in the Jewish manner, which would make this Saturday night, or from dawn, which would make it Sunday night. This is one of the earliest references to believers gathering on this day.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering, used that way in the preceding chapter, and the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is visible as one word.

notes.phrase: serving the Lord as a slave
notes.note: The verb is the one used for the service a slave owes a master, not a general word for serving. Most translations have simply 'serving', which loses the image of belonging wholly to the Lord. Some scholars note that 'slave of the Lord' also echoes an honorific Septuagint title for Moses and the prophets.

Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term understood to include a change of life. In modern English, however, the word centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct.

The Greek can mean that Paul is bound by the Holy Spirit, or that he is bound in his own spirit, that is, inwardly compelled. The mention of the Holy Spirit in the next verse favours the first, which most recent translations follow. 'Bound' anticipates the literal chains of the next verse.

notes.phrase: clean of the blood of all
notes.traditional: innocent of the blood of all
notes.note: The image is that of the watchman in Ezekiel 3 and 33: if he fails to sound the warning, the blood of those who die is on his hands. Paul claims to have discharged that responsibility, as he did with similar words at Corinth in Acts 18:6.

This is the word that later became 'bishop'. Here it is applied to the same people called 'elders' in verse 17, so the two terms describe one group of local leaders. It is not yet a distinct office above the elders.

The Greek can be read 'his own blood' or 'the blood of his own one', meaning his Son; 'his own' was a term of endearment for close kin. The traditional rendering takes it the first way, and many scholars and several recent translations take it the second. There is also a manuscript variant: some read 'the assembly of the Lord' instead of 'of God', which may have arisen to ease the difficulty of speaking of God's blood.

notes.phrase: It is more blessed to give than to receive
notes.note: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in any of the four Gospels. It is one of the few sayings attributed to him elsewhere in the New Testament, and shows that his words also circulated independently of the written Gospels.
